logs.search.results:
**No, you do not have to throw out rice after exactly 24 hours; this claim is inaccurate.** Cooked rice left at room temperature should not sit out for more than **2 hours** (or 1 hour if the temperature exceeds 90°F/32°C) to avoid bacterial growth like *Bacillus cereus*, which can cause food poisoning, but once refrigerated promptly, it lasts **3-6 days** in the fridge or up to **6-8 months** frozen.[1][2][3]

### Key Facts on Cooked Rice Safety and Storage
- **Room temperature limit**: Cool and refrigerate cooked rice within 2 hours of cooking to prevent toxins from *Bacillus cereus*; beyond this, discard it due to spoilage risk (not a strict 24-hour rule).[1][2]
- **Fridge lifespan**: Properly stored in an airtight container, cooked rice (white or brown) stays safe for 3-4 days (some sources say up to 6 days or a week).[1][2][3]
- **Freezer lifespan**: Freezes well for 6-8 months; thaw and reheat to at least 165°F (74°C).[2][3]
- **Spoilage signs**: Discard if you see mold, unusual smell, gooey texture, or discoloration.[2]

Sources confirming these guidelines:
- https://www.chicorice.com/blogs/all-about-rice/how-to-store-brown-rice ("Cooked brown rice left out for more than two hours... can grow bacteria"; fridge: 4-6 days)[1]
- https://www.healthline.com/nutrition/does-rice-go-bad ("Refrigerated within 2 hours"; fridge: 3-4 days or up to a week; freezer: 8 months)[2]
- https://www.mill.com/blog/does-rice-expire (USDA: fridge 3-4 days; freezer 8 months; quick refrigeration key)[3]

The 24-hour idea may stem from confusion between room-temp danger zone and fridge storage; official guidance prioritizes rapid cooling over a fixed 24-hour discard.[2][3]

logs.search.results:
**The meme's claim is false: Impeachment by the House without Senate conviction does not nullify a president's term or reset term limits under the U.S. Constitution, allowing no extra elections beyond the two-term limit in the 22nd Amendment.**

The **22nd Amendment** explicitly limits presidents to being elected no more than twice (or once if they've served more than two years of another president's term), with no provision linking impeachment outcomes to term resets: "No person shall be elected to the office of the President more than twice..." https://constitutioncenter.org/the-constitution/amendments/amendment-xxii[1]; https://constitution.congress.gov/constitution/amendment-22/[4].

**Impeachment rules** in Article II, Section 4 and Article I, Section 3 require removal from office only upon Senate conviction by a two-thirds vote; acquittal (as with both of Trump's impeachments) leaves the president in office, term intact, and eligible only for remaining allowed elections: "shall be removed from Office on Impeachment for, and Conviction of..." https://constitution.congress.gov/browse/essay/artII-S4-4-9/ALDE_00000035/[6]; https://www.senate.gov/about/powers-procedures/impeachment.htm[7]; https://www.law.cornell.edu/constitution-conan/article-1/section-3/clause-6/impeaching-the-president[5].

Fact-checks directly refute the exact claim, confirming no constitutional support for nullifying a term after House impeachment alone, as Trump remained eligible for (but did not pursue) a non-consecutive second term post-acquittals. https://www.theusconstitution.org/news/does-a-failed-impeachment-nullify-presidential-term-allow-extra-reelection/[3].
